title: Visakha's eight gifts
hookLine: a downpour, a mistaken servant, and eight gifts nobody else had thought of.
carry: visakha's giving: notice who got missed
tomorrow: if nobody is giving you orders, why keep a rule at all?

cards: On moving day, most friends bring boxes. One friend notices that nobody has eaten since breakfast. So what can you give in a single day that costs no money at all?
Drop into a downpour in the city of Savatthi. A servant girl runs back through the rain to her mistress, Visakha, with strange news.
She was sent to tell the monks their meal is ready, she says, but there are no monks at the monastery. Only naked ascetics, standing out in the rain.

teach.b: Visakha understands at once. The monks are bathing in the rain, and they have nothing to bathe in. She sends the girl back.
After the meal, as the monastic rule books tell it, she asks the Buddha for eight boons, gifts she'll give for as long as she lives. Cloths for the monks to bathe in when it rains.
Food for monks arriving in town, tired, who don't know the streets yet. Food for monks leaving, so they don't miss their caravan while begging. Food for the sick.
Food for whoever is nursing the sick, so they don't go hungry while caring. Medicine.
A steady supply of rice gruel. And bathing cloths for the nuns. The Buddha asks her why, and she has a reason for every one.
The food cost money. The noticing didn't. She saw the newcomer, the traveler, the patient, and the person everyone forgets: the one doing the caring.
That's the gift under all her gifts.
And it's what a day of giving can be. Time. Attention.
Food, if you have it. Praise, honestly meant. Visakha's eight boons start with her eyes.

how: Lay Buddhists give food, robes and medicine to monastics, and temples hold days of giving; teachers also name time, attention and kind speech as gifts anyone can give.

games.q: what does “a day of giving” mean?
o: a day when monks hand out gifts to their supporters
giving time, attention, food and praise where it's needed
a festival day when shops give away free goods

games.q: Visakha's eight boons — tap the pairs.
p: the monks had nothing to bathe in
they don't know the streets yet
so they don't miss their caravan
so they don't go hungry while caring

s: the servant girl thought the monks in the rain were naked ascetics
she came back saying there were no monks at the monastery. Visakha understood at once.
Visakha's food cost money; the noticing behind it didn't. time, attention and praise are gifts too.
Visakha's boons were all for the most senior monks
they went to newcomers, travelers, the sick, their nurses and the nuns.

games.q: a coworker is covering for a sick colleague and keeps skipping lunch. by Visakha's eight boons, who is the one people tend to forget here?
o: the sick colleague, who needs the most care.
the coworker doing the caring, who needs feeding too.
the manager, who has to sort out the schedule.
games.why: Visakha asked to feed whoever nurses the sick, so they don't go hungry while caring. the carer is easy to miss.

practice: Say softly, out loud, the name of one person you'll see today. Then name one thing they might need that nobody has noticed: a little time, real attention, a meal, an honest word of praise.
Sit with that person in mind, the way Visakha sat with the monks in the rain.

wordCard.voice: A day of giving: time, attention, food and praise, given where you've noticed the need. Visakha's eight boons began that way.

orig.note: Pali: Visakha, the laywoman who asked the Buddha for the eight boons.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: Visakha's giving, which starts with noticing who got missed. Talk tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.15 (Visakha's eight boons: rain-bathing cloths for the Sangha, food for incoming monks, food for outgoing monks, food for the sick, food for those who nurse the sick, medicine for the sick, a constant supply of rice gruel, bathing cloths for the nuns; the servant mistakes the monks bathing in the rain for naked ascetics; Visakha gives her reasons)
